prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, trapping atoms at a magic wavelength to reach unprecedented frequency accuracy and stability

statement.case_for: After reading the opening ballots I move B030 from third place to my preferred prize, and I do so on scientific grounds rather than because seven of eight members ranked it. It is the kind of experiment I value: a clean idea (the magic wavelength, which cancels the lattice light shift) followed by an implementation in which every physical detail (blackbody shift, collisional shifts, lattice light shifts, decoherence) is characterized until the clocks agree at the 1e-18 level. It has opened a regime that was not accessible before: relativistic redshift resolved over millimetres, searches for variation of constants and dark matter, and clock-based geodesy. It has been reproduced and surpassed in several independent laboratories (Tokyo/RIKEN, JILA, PTB, SYRTE, NIM and others), so the interpretation is stable. Attribution is unusually clean: Katori proposed the lattice-clock concept and demonstrated it, and Ye brought it to the highest accuracy and into the many-body regime. All seven members who ranked B030 independently proposed exactly this pair.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is partial overlap with earlier prizes in precision spectroscopy and frequency metrology: Hall and Hansch (2005, frequency combs) and Wineland (2012, ion control, including the Al+ optical clock). A skeptic can read the lattice clock as an extremely successful refinement of known ideas and technology rather than a new law or phenomenon. The work is also an instrument, and its largest promised payoff, the redefinition of the SI second and clock-based tests of new physics, is still ahead of us. Other groups with real claims (for example Lemke, Ludlow, Hinkley, Bloom, and the pioneers of the Yb clocks) are left out, and a two-person prize does not capture the full community. I weigh these as real but not decisive.

responses.point: Lindroth ranked B030 first on the grounds that the magic-wavelength idea rests on atomic polarizability physics and opened tests of fundamental physics nobody expected, while ranking Cirac-Zoller (B044) second as a theory prize that would need to be framed as such because the experimental realizations belong to Wineland, Blatt and Monroe.
responses.response: I agree on B030, and her atomic-structure expertise is the right check on my own more circuit-oriented reading. I also take her warning on B044 seriously. It moves me away from putting my own second-ranked candidate in the preferred configuration: a theory-only prize for ion-trap gates sits awkwardly beside the 2012 prize, which honoured the experiments, and I cannot easily justify it as a distinct achievement for this year. I keep it as an alternative, not a lead.

responses.point: Kroll also ranked B030 first, stressing that the clock changed what can be measured (relativistic geodesy, constants, dark-matter searches) and that several independent laboratories have confirmed and surpassed the early results. He placed the Higgs experiments (B017) seventh and IceCube (B020) eighth, on attribution and timing grounds.
responses.response: I agree with the main point, and the independence of the confirming laboratories is what persuades me that this is robust rather than one group's achievement. I also share his hesitation on collaboration prizes: where credit is collective, any three-person configuration is arbitrary. That is a significant point in favour of a prize whose attribution is as clean as it is for Katori and Ye.

responses.point: Eriksson put topological insulators (B058) first, as a theory-then-experiment case (Kane and Mele, with Molenkamp's HgTe observation) that opened a class of matter with protected edge states. He ranked B030 fourth and B057 third.
responses.response: The Kane-Mele-Molenkamp story is a genuine discovery of a new class of matter and the experimental confirmation was fast. I defer to him on the materials physics. My qualification is the 2016 prize for topological phases, which makes B058 closer to a sequel than a new regime, and I think the committee must decide whether it wants to return to topology this soon. I place the clock ahead of it because the whole accuracy chain is understood in detail and was confirmed in many laboratories, but I accept that this is a judgment about different kinds of discovery and not a measurable ordering.

responses.point: Pearce ranked IceCube (B020) first as a landmark of detector-driven astroparticle physics that opened neutrino astronomy, with Halzen, Karle and Spiering as the architects, and ranked B030 fifth.
responses.response: The opening of a new observational window is an impressive achievement and I do not dispute its importance. Astroparticle physics is outside my competence, so I defer to him on how well Karle and Spiering can be separated from the hundreds of collaborators. Two things keep me from ranking it first: the source identification (TXS 0506+056, NGC 1068, the Galactic plane) is still developing, and attribution in a large collaboration rests on judgments about leadership roles. Neither is a flaw in the discovery. If the committee prefers a discovery of nature to an instrument invention, B020 is the strongest competitor, and I would not oppose a split prize on those lines.

responses.point: Olsson ranked the Higgs discovery (B017) first as the decisive experimental verification of mass generation, a discovery of the kind the statutes name, while acknowledging that the credited list exceeds three people and ranked B030 last of her ranked candidates (eighth).
responses.response: I agree that the Higgs discovery is the most unambiguous in importance, and I ranked it fifth only because it is outside my field. My reservation is attribution rather than merit: with spokespeople, detector leaders and the LHC director all plausible, a three-name selection will be contested whatever we choose. I would like to hear from the particle physicists whether a defensible trio exists, because if it does, the case for a particle-physics prize this year is strong and I would not claim that the clock outweighs it.

uncertainties: Whether the committee views the overlap with the 2005 (frequency comb) and 2012 (Wineland, ion clocks) prizes as a reason to wait, or considers the lattice clock a distinct achievement.
Whether a defensible three-name configuration exists for B017 (Higgs) or B020 (IceCube) that would make a collaboration-based discovery preferable to an instrument invention this year.
Whether the redefinition of the SI second, if it happens soon, would strengthen the case for B030 further or whether recognition should come first.
Whether B044 (Cirac and Zoller) can be justified as a theory prize distinct from Wineland's 2012 recognition and from the 2022 prize on entanglement experiments.
statement.conflict_note: I am Director of the Wallenberg Centre for Quantum Technology and a theorist in superconducting circuits, so I have a clear connection to B029 (circuit QED) and to a lesser extent B044 (quantum computing theory); I would recuse myself or at minimum discount my own ranking of B029, whose field also received the 2025 prize. I have no personal or institutional connection to Katori, Ye or the clock groups that is apparent from my profile.
